verification.reason: The union over every stage's tier is the base behaviour (base doctor.ts:127). The head only adds a label and a comment. The head comment says the no-target plan is "over every stage's checks" (lines 120-123). That is a deliberate superset, so doctor warns about any stage's lenses, as the earlier comment describes ("a tier a stage's lenses run on"). I found no active decision or documented design text that forbids this or requires the no-target plan to use only the pull-request tier. The cli.md `doctor` row says "With no argument the plan is a range review's on the checked-out commit". That describes the plan's source (working tree and preferences). It does not say which stage tier supplies the checks. The words "never a second reading of the configuration" apply to `melian doctor <target>`, which does use `ReviewTarget.plan` and the pull-request tier. The claim names no decision it contradicts. The mismatch it describes is real but narrow: with divergent stage tiers, a doctor plan that includes a lens the pull-request tier omits. It is not a contradiction of documented words, so this rule's bar is not met.

The base rejects a doctor target, and two active decisions forbid one. At base, main.ts line 487 throws "doctor takes no arguments". The active restore-doctor-clauses decision says "Doctor has no pull request argument" (line 18). The active doctor-github-read-deadline decision says doctor "never fetches" (line 5). The head adds a target argument. `planChecks` calls `ReviewTarget.resolve`, which calls `gitHubFor` and then `fetchedPullRequest`. The fetch runs `git fetch` with no deadline and moves the local pr refs. Only the viewer and permission read has the ten-second deadline. A planChecks failure with a target becomes a "fail" check (doctor.ts line 172), so a missing token makes doctor fail instead of warn. The first scenario depends on a transport that hangs. I traced the other behaviours in code.

evidence.snippet: [Issue #614](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/614) makes `melian doctor` answer for one review. Before this, doctor printed the plan from the working tree and the preference files. A pull request's review reads its policy and lenses from its base, so on [pull request #532](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/pull/532) a lens route in an uncommitted `melian.local.yaml` printed as applying while the round ran the committed model, and two reruns went by before anyone knew. `melian doctor <target>` now takes a target as `review` does, `"#12"` or a range. It prints that review's plan from `ReviewTarget`, which `review` now resolves its changeset, policy source, lenses, policy and tier checks through too, so the two cannot drift. A first `plan` line names the review and where it reads its policy. When the review reads a revision, a warning names each preference file it ignores, `melian.local.yaml` or the user's own. With no target, doctor keeps its plan and says it is a range review's on the checked-out commit. A target doctor cannot resolve fails the `plan` line. `packages/cli/test/doctor-target.test.ts` failed first at `origin/main` c2e68c4e: doctor printed the local route for `"#7"` and named no review. It now covers a pull request, the user's preference file, a range with its head checked out and one without, and a target that cannot be resolved. The [cli guideline](../guidelines/cli.md), the [design](../design.md), the three skills and the AGENTS.md learning on routing a lens past Codex's content filter now say which plan doctor prints for which target. The change guards no trust or durability property: doctor decides nothing, so no mutation inventory is owed.

## The rule

- A builder owes the enumeration-first inventory, with every claimed mutant run by hand, only for changed code that guards trust or durability.
- Trust code decides who or what Melian trusts, what a verdict blocks, what runs with a credential or outside a sandbox, or what a key matches. Durability code writes or migrates a stored shape, resumes after a crash, or publishes.
- Every other change owes no inventory. Its fix starts with a failing test, its new behaviour has a test, and the tests lens reports `untested-behaviour` at its usual severity.
- The pull request's description lists its changed files that guard trust or durability, or says there are none. The review of record checks that list against the diff, and a file left off it is a P2 finding.
- The interim rule and convergence rule 2 now read: a fix pass proves its own commits' mutants in code that guards trust or durability, and owes none elsewhere. A shared test suite owes the proof the suite decision describes only when the port it tests is trust or durability code.
- The inventory is the enumerator's whole output for the range, unedited, so its total still checks itself, and no one deletes rows by hand. A claim is owed on every row in the listed files and on no other row, once the sampler can read which files those are ([issue #418](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/418)). Until then a pull request that owes an inventory claims every row, as before, so the review of record's `--sample` runs unchanged.
- An inventory already written for a pull request in flight stands for the code it covers, and no one extends it to ordinary code. A later commit on that pull request that changes trust or durability code still appends and proves its own mutants, as every fix pass does.

verification.reason: The sentence is not an injection. It is the ordinary closing line of a progress-log entry. It reports the author's classification under the active decision "The hand mutation proof is owed only for code that guards trust or durability". That decision says every other change owes no inventory and that the pull request says which changed files guard trust or durability, or says there are none. The sentence addresses no reviewer or tool, issues no instruction, and tries to change no behaviour. The decision also says the review of record checks that list against the diff, so a reviewer still judges the claim independently. At most the classification could be wrong, because `review` now resolves policy source through `ReviewTarget`. That would be a misclassification finding under the decision's own rule, not an injection attempt.
